lines.text: A land of black earth and wide steppe, fought over by empires, starved, poisoned and invaded, and still standing. This is the story of Ukraine.
To the south lies the Black Sea, which turned salt again as the oceans rose after the last ice age, about eight thousand years ago.
On the land above it, Trypillian farmers of the Stone Age built towns that were among the largest anywhere in Europe.
By tradition Kyiv was founded in the late fifth century, the city later called the mother of the cities of Rus.
In the late eight hundreds it became the centre of Kievan Rus, a union of Slavic princedoms that Ukrainians, Russians and Belarusians all claim as their root.
Around 988 its prince, Volodymyr the Great, was baptised, and Rus became Orthodox Christian.
Soon after, in the early ten hundreds, Kyiv began its great Saint Sophia Cathedral, a sign of a capital to rival any in Europe.
Monks dug into the hills above the Dnipro and founded the Monastery of the Caves, the Pechersk Lavra, still a centre of faith.
After the Mongols sacked Kyiv and Poland-Lithuania ruled, the Cossacks rose. In 1648 Bohdan Khmelnytsky led them in a great revolt.
From that rising came the Cossack Hetmanate, a state of their own, until Russia drew most of the land into its empire.
Under the tsars, Taras Shevchenko, born a serf, became a poet and painter, the father of Ukrainian literature.
When the Russian Empire collapsed in 1917, Ukrainians fought for a country of their own, a struggle that lasted four years.
That was the first modern Ukraine, a large land of rich farms that would win full independence only in 1991.
The Ukrainian People's Republic held out from 1917 to 1921, before the Soviets won and the state was crushed.
In 1932 and 1933, under Stalin, grain was taken and farms were forced together. Millions starved in the Holodomor, which many countries call a genocide.
Then the Nazis came. In September 1941, at the ravine of Babi Yar outside Kyiv, more than thirty thousand Jews were shot in two days.
After the war, in 1970, the Soviets built Pripyat, a town of some fifty thousand people for the workers of a new nuclear plant.
Andriy Shevchenko, born in 1976, would grow up to be a great striker and win the Ballon d'Or in 2004.
And Volodymyr Zelenskyy, born in 1978, would go from comic actor to president, and lead his country at war.
In April 1986 a reactor at Chernobyl exploded, spreading radiation across Europe. Tens of thousands of people had to leave their homes.
Pripyat has stood empty ever since, inside a closed zone where forests and wildlife have slowly taken back the land.
On the twenty-fourth of August 1991, as the Soviet Union fell apart, Ukraine declared its independence.
In 1994 it gave up the world's third largest nuclear arsenal, in return for promises that it would be safe.
In 2004, when a presidential vote was rigged, crowds in orange filled the streets. The vote was held again, and Viktor Yushchenko won.
In 2013 the government dropped a deal with the European Union. Protest on Kyiv's Maidan became a revolution, and the president fled.
Russia answered with war, and in 2014 the fighting began, in Crimea and in the Donbas.
That spring Russia seized Crimea and claimed it as its own.
Then, in February 2022, Russia launched a full invasion, killing many and driving millions from their homes.
In the south, Russian forces besieged Mariupol and left the city in ruins.
But in the north, the attack on Kyiv failed, and the capital held.
In June 2023 the great Kakhovka Dam on the Dnipro was blown up, flooding the towns downstream.
From Trypillia to today, Ukraine's story is still being fought for.
